guide.title: Stolen routes, the guide
guide.subtitle: How a route is hijacked on the Internet, and how a detector catches it.
guide.intro.map: This is the guide, to read from top to bottom. The application holds the same figures, one per screen: the simulator, the 2008 incident, the prefixes, the lookup. The references gather the readings for learning BGP, in the order worth reading them.
guide.intro.p1: On 24 February 2008, one BGP announcement for a block of 256 addresses diverted YouTube's traffic worldwide, and it was withdrawn only two and a quarter hours later. No router broke the protocol: BGP has no way to check whether a network has the right to announce a prefix.
guide.intro.p2: This page starts from a simulator with real routers, running right now: three FRR routers, an attacker triggered on demand and a detector that listens to everything. Then comes the same 2008 hijack, replayed from the data recorded at the time, the history of every watched prefix, and a lookup of any real prefix on the Internet.

guide.s1.p1: The Internet is a sum of independent networks, <dfn class="term" data-term="as" tabindex="0" role="button">autonomous systems</dfn>, each with a number. Each one <dfn class="term" data-term="announcement" tabindex="0" role="button">announces</dfn> to its neighbours, over <dfn class="term" data-term="bgp" tabindex="0" role="button">BGP</dfn>, the <dfn class="term" data-term="prefix" tabindex="0" role="button">prefixes</dfn> it holds, and the neighbours pass the announcement on, adding their number to the <dfn class="term" data-term="as_path" tabindex="0" role="button">AS path</dfn>. The last number of the path is the <dfn class="term" data-term="origin" tabindex="0" role="button">origin</dfn>, the network that claims to hold the prefix.
guide.s1.p2: The simulator holds three such networks. The victim (AS65001) holds the prefix 203.0.113.0/24 and announces it. The transit (AS65000) is the provider that passes on everything it receives, exactly like a real provider. The attacker (AS65003) has a session with the transit and, at first, announces nothing. A collector listens to all three routers and hands every message to the detector.
guide.fig1.title: Figure 1. The simulator, live
guide.fig1.note: three real FRR routers, read every two seconds
guide.s1.p3: Each router picks a single route for a prefix. Given two announcements for the same prefix, it prefers the path with fewer autonomous systems, and on a tie it keeps the older one. When two prefixes overlap, packets follow the more specific one, the sub-prefix. Press “Hijack” and watch the tables in the inspector: the false announcement for the /24 stays a backup route on the transit, but the /25 has no rival and is chosen everywhere.
guide.s1.p4: The map shows the three autonomous systems, the BGP sessions between the routers and the collector. When a table changes, UPDATE messages leave the origin and travel from router to router, then each router tells the collector what it chose. Every hop is an event: the bar under the map plays them at the chosen speed and shows the current one, “Step” makes one hop, “Back” undoes it, and in the inspector's “Events” tab a click on an event jumps to it. “Send the packet” follows a packet to the chosen address: at each router the route with the most specific prefix wins, and its next hop says where the packet goes. The address 203.0.113.1 lies in the sub-prefix the attacker announces; 203.0.113.129 does not. During the hijack the first reaches the attacker and is dropped on a blackhole route, while the second still reaches the victim.
guide.s1.p5: The simulated packet reads the BGP tables; “Ask the kernels” checks it: each router answers with its real routing decision for the same address, hop by hop. On the lab's shared segment a route's next hop can be the origin router itself, so the attacker sends the victim's packets without passing through the transit, and the kernels confirm it.
guide.s2.p1: The detector knows beforehand who may announce each watched prefix. For every announcement it receives it makes three checks: the exact prefix announced by another origin is a false origin; a more specific prefix inside a watched one, with another origin, is a hijacked sub-prefix; an announcement that no RPKI authorisation allows is RPKI-invalid. The alerts of the same hijack, seen from several vantage points, form an incident.
guide.fig2.title: Figure 2. The incidents
guide.fig2.note: click an incident to see what it means
guide.fig2.raw: Raw data: the incidents and the latest 200 alerts
guide.s3.p1: AS17557 (Pakistan Telecom) announced 208.65.153.0/24, a sub-prefix of the 208.65.152.0/22 block announced by YouTube (AS36561). Its provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), passed the announcement on, and within two minutes the route had reached every RIPE RIS collector. Being more specific, it drew the traffic wherever it was accepted. YouTube answered after about 80 minutes with its own /24, then with two /25 prefixes, and PCCW withdrew the routes at 21:01 UTC.
guide.s3.p2: Here the detector receives exactly the messages the rrc00 collector recorded at the time, from the public MRT files, with 208.65.152.0/22 as the watched prefix and AS36561 as the legitimate origin. The alert appears in the second of the sub-prefix's first announcement, at 18:47:57 UTC.
guide.fig3.title: Figure 3. The YouTube hijack, as the neighbours of the rrc00 collector saw it
guide.fig3.caption: One row per neighbour of the collector: the lane shows where it sent the traffic for the hijacked block (red, AS17557; green, AS36561), and on the right the AS path at the chosen moment, with the autonomous system that hands the route to the origin framed. The numbered dotted lines are the documented events and cut the axis into phases: each phase is as wide as the square root of its duration, with the real duration written above it, so the three minutes before stay visible and the 80 compressed minutes of the hijack carry the // mark. The bar under the lanes scrubs through the incident, and “Play” runs it.
guide.s4.p1: Every announcement and every withdrawal the collector receives is kept in the database, with the prefix in a native type that supports containment searches. For a watched prefix, the page shows the route each vantage point holds now and every moment the route changed.
guide.fig4.title: Figure 4. The history of a prefix
guide.fig4.note: one row for each router and prefix seen
guide.s5.p1: RPKI is the Internet's answer to the problem above: the holder of an address block signs an authorisation (ROA) that says which AS may announce the prefix and up to what length. A validating router usually rejects an invalid announcement. In the simulator, the authorisation says that only AS65001 may announce 203.0.113.0/24, with a maximum length of 24, which is why the attacker's /25 is invalid too. The data below comes on request from RIPEstat, the RIPE NCC's public data service.
guide.fig5.title: Figure 5. A real prefix, today
guide.s6.p1: Further: the references, the readings ordered in stages, with the lineage of the BGP specification from RFC 1105 to RFC 4271; and the RIPE NCC's 2008 case study, the source of the timeline in Figure 3.
guide.s6.p2: The simulator is a closed network with no uplink: private AS numbers, the documentation prefix 203.0.113.0/24 (RFC 5737), nothing leaves the machine. The hijack is a test, replayed on request. The lookup in Figure 5 is the only request to the Internet, and it only reads.

js.term.as.title: Autonomous system (AS)
js.term.as.body: A network run by a single organisation, identified by a number: AS3333 is the RIPE NCC, AS65001 is the simulator's victim. The Internet is made of tens of thousands of such networks telling one another which addresses they hold.
js.term.prefix.title: Prefix
js.term.prefix.body: A block of IP addresses written as an address and a length: 203.0.113.0/24 means the 256 addresses that start with 203.0.113. The longer the length, the smaller and more specific the block.
js.term.bgp.title: BGP
js.term.bgp.body: Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol through which autonomous systems announce their prefixes and learn where to send traffic. A BGP router does not check whether its neighbour has the right to announce what it announces.
js.term.update.title: UPDATE message
js.term.update.body: The BGP message that announces or withdraws prefixes. It carries the prefixes and the path attributes, among them the list of autonomous systems crossed.
js.term.as_path.title: AS path
js.term.as_path.body: The list of autonomous systems an announcement has passed through. Each AS adds its number at the front when it passes the announcement on, so the last number is the origin.
js.term.origin.title: Origin
js.term.origin.body: The AS that started the announcement of a prefix, the last one of the AS path. A false origin is an AS that announces a prefix that does not belong to it.
js.term.announcement.title: Announcement
js.term.announcement.body: An AS's claim, sent over BGP, that it can deliver traffic to a prefix. The neighbours believe it and pass it on, unless their policy rejects it.
js.term.subprefix.title: Sub-prefix
js.term.subprefix.body: A more specific prefix inside another: 203.0.113.0/25 is half of 203.0.113.0/24. Routers send packets along the most specific prefix, so a sub-prefix announced by an attacker wins wherever it arrives.
js.term.hijack.title: Route hijack
js.term.hijack.body: An AS announces a prefix that does not belong to it, or a sub-prefix of it, and draws the traffic meant for the owner. It can be an attack or a configuration mistake; routers cannot tell the difference.
js.term.rpki.title: RPKI and ROA
js.term.rpki.body: Resource Public Key Infrastructure: the holder of an address block signs an authorisation (ROA) that says which AS may announce the prefix and up to what length. A validating router classifies every route as valid, invalid or not found.
js.term.vantage.title: Vantage point
js.term.vantage.body: A router from which the collector receives announcements. A false announcement reaches only part of the networks, which is why the detector listens to several points at once.
js.term.collector.title: Collector
js.term.collector.body: A process the routers report their routes to, only so they can be listened to. In the simulator, each router sends it, over BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol, RFC 7854), the routes it chose; the collector announces nothing, and everything it receives goes to the detector. RIPE RIS and RouteViews are public collectors, which receive routes over BGP sessions.
js.term.mrt.title: MRT
js.term.mrt.body: The file format in which public collectors archive BGP messages (RFC 6396). This project's parser reads them directly.
js.term.ris.title: RIPE RIS
js.term.ris.body: Routing Information Service, the RIPE NCC's public collectors. Their files of 24 February 2008 are the ones replayed on this page.
js.term.next_hop.title: Next hop
js.term.next_hop.body: The address of the neighbour a router sends a prefix's packets to. On a shared segment an announcement can keep the next hop of the original route, so the packet bypasses the router that passed it on.
js.term.blackhole.title: Blackhole route
js.term.blackhole.body: A route that drops packets instead of forwarding them. The simulator's attacker uses one for the hijacked prefixes, as happened to YouTube's traffic in 2008.

js.outcome.dropped: The packet vanishes: it was drawn to a router that drops it.

js.outcome.lost: The packet leaves for a router that is not in the simulator.
js.outcome.loop: The packet goes round in a loop.
js.outcome.unknown: An answer the page does not understand.
js.kernel.local: delivers the packet locally: the address is its own
js.kernel.direct: delivers the packet straight onto the link
js.kernel.blackhole: drops the packet: its route is a blackhole
js.kernel.agrees: The kernels confirm the simulation on the BGP tables: the same routers, the same outcome.
js.kernel.disagrees: The kernels say something other than the simulation: the tables changed in the meantime or the kernel routes differently.

js.sim.done.ask: The kernels answered; no packet was sent.

js.explain.origin: {origin} announces the prefix {monitored} as if it were its own, but the known legitimate origin is {expected}. The routers that choose this announcement send the traffic to AS{asn}, not to the owner.
js.explain.subprefix: {origin} announces {subs}, a more specific part of {monitored}{owner}. Routers always choose the most specific route, so the announcement beats the legitimate route wherever it arrives.
js.explain.rpki: The announcements contradict RPKI: no route origin authorisation (ROA) allows AS{asn} to announce these prefixes at these lengths. A router that validates origins usually rejects such routes.
js.explain.seen: The collector saw the announcement from {vantages}: {peers}. {alerts} in all; their rows are under “Raw data”.
js.prefix.hijacked.router.one: Now {wrong} of {total} router has a route with an origin other than {origins}: {list}.
js.prefix.hijacked.router.many: Now {wrong} of {total} routers have a route with an origin other than {origins}: {list}.
js.prefix.hijacked.peer.one: Now {wrong} of {total} RIS neighbour has a route with an origin other than {origins}: {list}.
js.prefix.hijacked.peer.many: Now {wrong} of {total} RIS neighbours have a route with an origin other than {origins}: {list}.
js.prefix.legit.router.one: Now the only router sends {prefix} to {origins}, the expected origin.
js.prefix.legit.router.many: Now all {total} routers send {prefix} to {origins}, the expected origin.
js.prefix.legit.peer.one: Now the only RIS neighbour sends {prefix} to {origins}, the expected origin.
js.prefix.legit.peer.many: Now all {total} RIS neighbours send {prefix} to {origins}, the expected origin.
js.prefix.legend: Lane: green = to {origins}, red = to another AS, line = no route
js.prefix.path.at: AS path at {time} UTC, towards the origin
js.prefix.path.now: AS path now, towards the origin
js.prefix.none.this: No route seen for this prefix.
js.prefix.more: The latest {shown} of {total}; all of them are under “Raw data”.
js.lookup.server: The public address of the machine that serves the page.
js.rpki.sentence.valid: {prefix} is announced by {by}, and the origin is authorised.
js.rpki.sentence.invalid: {prefix} is announced by {by}, but the published authorisations do not allow this announcement.
js.rpki.sentence.not-found: {prefix} is announced by {by}; the holder has published no RPKI authorisation.
js.rpki.sentence.unknown: {prefix} is announced by {by}; RIPEstat could not evaluate RPKI.
js.rpki.meaning.valid: the prefix's holder has published in RPKI that {asns} may announce it. An announcement of the same prefix from another AS would be RPKI-invalid, and the networks that filter would reject it.
js.rpki.meaning.invalid: the announcement contradicts the authorisations its holder published: the origin or the prefix length does not match. Networks that validate RPKI reject it; it is the typical sign of a hijack or a configuration error.
js.rpki.meaning.not-found: without an authorisation RPKI cannot say anything: an announcement of the same prefix from another AS would be accepted just as easily. Every prefix was like this in 2008, before RPKI.
js.rpki.meaning.unknown: RIPEstat returned no RPKI state for this prefix; a later attempt may succeed.
js.roa.invalid_length: the announcement is longer than it allows
js.lookup.unannounced: {resource} is not announced in BGP now: no public route covers it.
